 TOWARD A CULTURAL AND INTELLECTUAL HISTORY OF SOVIET RUSSIA IN THE 1920 s

 Some Preliminary Directions for a Réévaluation of Politics and Culture*

 MARK VON HAGEN

### The 1920s as 'Golden Age' and the Historiography of the New Economic Policy (NEP)

 In western historiography the now prédominant interprétation of culture in the 1920s has représentée! it as a golden age when the Bolshevik régime tole- rated a cultural pluralism that gave rise to some of the greatest contributions that Russia has made to world culture, most particularly in the avant-garde. That golden age came to an abrupt hait at the end of the 1920s and beginning of the 1930s when Stalin and his henchmen choked off ail créative developments and led Russia into an iron age of stérile socialist realism, conformism, and mediocrity.1

* These reflections are intended to be suggestive and spéculative, not conclusive or authoritative. They hâve been provoked, in the best sensé of that term, by my long-term rea- ding of some refreshingly innovative essays and books by Kateřina Clark, The Soviet Novel, Chicago, 1981; and her Petersburg: Crucible of Cultural Révolution, Harvard, 1995; Jeffrey Brooks, When Russia Learned to Read, Princeton, 1985; Sheila Fitzpatrick, The Cultural Front, Ithaca, 1992; Boris Thomson, Lot's Wife and the Venus ofMilo, Cambridge, 1978; and Richard Stites, Revolutionary Dreams: Utopian Vision and Expérimental Life in the Russian Révolution, Oxford, 1989. In addition my thinking has been influenced by the literature on popular culture and on the relationships between politics and culture, including that by Fredric Jameson, Antonio Gramsci, Michel Foucault, and the Russian and Soviet formalists, structu- ralists, and semioticians. The original version of these reflections appeared as an effort to summarize a course I taught together with Robert Maguire, whose book on the thick journal Red Virgin Soil (Princeton, 1968) was itself a model of intellectual and cultural history through the prism of one institution's history; that original version was modified after I taught the course again several years later, this time together with Rosalinde Sartorti at the Ost- europa-Institut of the Free University Berlin. (Thanks to her and Markus Wehner's gallant efforts to render this text into German, it was much improved in the English édition.) Finally, these reflections émerge from my own research on the early history of the Red Army and its contributions to the culture of the 1920s and 1930s (Soldiers in the Proletarian Dictatorship, Ithaca, 1991).
